full_text: Dear Editor, Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) is coming of age and is poised to develop into a serious candidate for Point‐of‐care diagnostics. RPA has been around for almost 20 years. Originally developed by academics Nial Armes and Olaf Piepenburg, it was first published in 2006, and a first patent was issued in 2007. In the first decade of the 2000s, several isothermal molecular amplification methods emerged [1] but real‐time RPA stood out at the time as its design format was reminiscent of real‐time PCR (two primers and a probe). The probe used to confirm specific amplification was intuitively easier to accept than the backfolding FIP/BIB primers of Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP), which in essence do the same. To this day, this misunderstanding of the LAMP mechanism still leads to the development of additional real‐time probe system for LAMP in order to add a confirmatory probe [2, 3, 4, 5]. This may, however, also be the case because of the well‐documented unspecific amplification issues of LAMP [6]. In terms of sensitivity, both LAMP and RPA have been shown to be as sensitive as real‐time PCR in numerous studies; RT‐RPA, however, sometimes struggles in the last decade of sensitivity. An intriguing recent analysis speculates that, in contrast to fully biphasic UvsX‐GP32 droplets formed in the RPA reaction, the addition of RT leads to fully miscible droplets including BsuI, which inhibits UvsX and thus may cause the loss of sensitivity in RT‐RPA [7]. Both LAMP and RPA struggle with one tube multiplexing but the introduction of cascade amplification using CRISPR/Cas12 and 13 systems which digest ssDNA or ssRNA reports offers solutions but the most promising appear to be spatial multiplexing concepts on surfaces or digital droplets. From the onset RPA was available in lyophilised pellets for DNA and RNA targets which made it a popular choice for research into cold chain independent point of care diagnostics [8]. Other features included the speed of amplification to the analytical limit of detection from 5 to 20 min at very low temperatures. The low reaction temperature generically implies a reduced engineering effort and associated costs for a POCT device and even inspired some assay developments with body heat driven RPA [9]. Over the years RPA was implemented in a plethora of microfluidic devices [10]. During the Covid pandemic, widespread testing outside of centralised laboratories provided advantages for general epidemic control and contact tracing in particular and has changed attitudes towards POCT [11]. Subsequently, the FDA invited the diagnostic industry to submit tests for home testing and most recently approved a PCR home test by US Company Visby Medical Inc. for sexually transmitted diseases. It uses a disposable heavily engineered “device‐cartridge” with embedded electronics to steer a continuous flow heated serpentine PCR channel which seems a waste to dispose of after one test (patent US20250128262A1). Another disposable electronics concept was the much simpler LUCIRA device for a SARS‐CoV‐2 LAMP assay [12]. Marketed as device‐free disposable tests, both POCTs in truth generate electronic waste and do not meet the last E in the RERASSURED criteria which stands for “Equipment free or simple environmentally friendly” [13]. Only recently cost efficient and scalable simple multi use POCT devices have emerged such as the CPod (CRISPR assay [14]), minoo (RPA assay [15]), and Pebble device (LAMP assay [16]). CPod and minoo use a Light Emitting Diode (LED) and the onboard multi‐spectral digital sensor AS7341, for fluorescence detection while the Pebble uses a mini digital camera to detect a colorimetric reaction. The minoo device received CE‐IVD legacy certification in May 2022 for a SARS‐CoV‐2 RT‐RPA assay using a simple extraction procedure for throat swabs. While many others have created similar direct extraction concepts e.g., using TCEP buffer for SHERLOCK and LAMP assays [17, 18, 19], the bottleneck extraction for more complicated sample types is still not solved. In terms of multiplexing, the Biofire FilmArray system for multiplex PCR [20] has already demonstrated that spatial multiplexing is preferential to one‐pot multiplexing, which is true for the workload needed to balance one‐pot reactions and for the verification and validation effort for one‐pot reactions versus spatially separated individual reactions. It is therefore to be expected that the simple multi use POCT devices will also move in this direction. Only a few device publications have listed cost of goods (CoGS) for isothermal and portable PCR devices (range 50–193$ per device [21, 22]), therefore, with a margin added it is safe to estimate the CoGs within 250€ for the above devices. They can be categorized as environmentally friendly as at least the minoo device was verified to be functional for at least 1000 runs [15]. If they solve the extraction issue, these simple readers could help to provide molecular diagnostics for infectious agents to the 47% of the global population that has little to no access to diagnostics at all, thus solving the last mile problem in providing access to diagnostics close to the patient [23]. In principle, these test platforms would be deliverable to users at reduced sales prices if upscaled production was outsourced to international electronics/mobile phone manufacturers. Local biochemistry production would allow dissemination of affordable respective assays close to the WHO requirement of 1$/test [13]. In comparison, current microfluidic and microsystem POCT systems in general fail to consider the economy of scale for mass production and market [24]. RPA has been rated as the most promising isothermal molecular amplification technique since it utilizes unmodified oligonucleotides, rapidly amplifies targets at only slightly elevated temperature without compromising the stringency of amplification, and uses probe‐based target verification in its real time format [1]. A meta‐analysis of molecular POC assays for SARS‐CoV‐2 concluded that seven RT‐RPA/RAA assays achieved detection sensitivity level similar to diagnosis on purified RNA samples by PCR from crude patient samples [25]. RPA was used in multiple field studies in mobile laboratories and produced sufficient evidence demonstrating that the performance of RPA is suitable for point of care use. In view of original RPA patents running out in 2026 the first open‐source protocols for RPA mix production have been published [26, 27]. Apart from the original Twist DX kit which currently is not available for RNA detection, three RPA copy chemistries are available in China: Recombinase Aided Amplification (RAA [28], Qitian, https://en.qt‐bio.com/Pro/12.html), Enzymatic Recombinase Amplification (ERA [29], GenDX, https://www.igeneye.com/), and Multienzyme Isothermal Rapid Amplification (MIRA [30], Amp‐Future Biotech Co. Ltd. https://www.amp‐futurebio.com/products). The impetus to copy the successful RPA concept goes even as far as claiming to have invented a probe system which is identical to the one originally published in 2006 [31]. In the area of lateral flow detection RPA is beginning to overtake LAMP with 490 publications versus 412 recorded on PubMed. Taken together RPA is catching up on LAMP (Figure 1) and has the potential to develop into a serious candidate for POCT implementation which is certainly the view in Asia as 61% of RPA publications originate from China alone. full_text_sections.full_text: Dear Editor, Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) is coming of age and is poised to develop into a serious candidate for Point‐of‐care diagnostics. RPA has been around for almost 20 years. Originally developed by academics Nial Armes and Olaf Piepenburg, it was first published in 2006, and a first patent was issued in 2007. In the first decade of the 2000s, several isothermal molecular amplification methods emerged [1] but real‐time RPA stood out at the time as its design format was reminiscent of real‐time PCR (two primers and a probe). The probe used to confirm specific amplification was intuitively easier to accept than the backfolding FIP/BIB primers of Loop Mediated Isothermal Amplification (LAMP), which in essence do the same. To this day, this misunderstanding of the LAMP mechanism still leads to the development of additional real‐time probe system for LAMP in order to add a confirmatory probe [2, 3, 4, 5]. This may, however, also be the case because of the well‐documented unspecific amplification issues of LAMP [6]. In terms of sensitivity, both LAMP and RPA have been shown to be as sensitive as real‐time PCR in numerous studies; RT‐RPA, however, sometimes struggles in the last decade of sensitivity. An intriguing recent analysis speculates that, in contrast to fully biphasic UvsX‐GP32 droplets formed in the RPA reaction, the addition of RT leads to fully miscible droplets including BsuI, which inhibits UvsX and thus may cause the loss of sensitivity in RT‐RPA [7]. Both LAMP and RPA struggle with one tube multiplexing but the introduction of cascade amplification using CRISPR/Cas12 and 13 systems which digest ssDNA or ssRNA reports offers solutions but the most promising appear to be spatial multiplexing concepts on surfaces or digital droplets. From the onset RPA was available in lyophilised pellets for DNA and RNA targets which made it a popular choice for research into cold chain independent point of care diagnostics [8]. Other features included the speed of amplification to the analytical limit of detection from 5 to 20 min at very low temperatures. The low reaction temperature generically implies a reduced engineering effort and associated costs for a POCT device and even inspired some assay developments with body heat driven RPA [9]. Over the years RPA was implemented in a plethora of microfluidic devices [10]. During the Covid pandemic, widespread testing outside of centralised laboratories provided advantages for general epidemic control and contact tracing in particular and has changed attitudes towards POCT [11]. Subsequently, the FDA invited the diagnostic industry to submit tests for home testing and most recently approved a PCR home test by US Company Visby Medical Inc. for sexually transmitted diseases. It uses a disposable heavily engineered “device‐cartridge” with embedded electronics to steer a continuous flow heated serpentine PCR channel which seems a waste to dispose of after one test (patent US20250128262A1). Another disposable electronics concept was the much simpler LUCIRA device for a SARS‐CoV‐2 LAMP assay [12]. Marketed as device‐free disposable tests, both POCTs in truth generate electronic waste and do not meet the last E in the RERASSURED criteria which stands for “Equipment free or simple environmentally friendly” [13]. Only recently cost efficient and scalable simple multi use POCT devices have emerged such as the CPod (CRISPR assay [14]), minoo (RPA assay [15]), and Pebble device (LAMP assay [16]). CPod and minoo use a Light Emitting Diode (LED) and the onboard multi‐spectral digital sensor AS7341, for fluorescence detection while the Pebble uses a mini digital camera to detect a colorimetric reaction. The minoo device received CE‐IVD legacy certification in May 2022 for a SARS‐CoV‐2 RT‐RPA assay using a simple extraction procedure for throat swabs. While many others have created similar direct extraction concepts e.g., using TCEP buffer for SHERLOCK and LAMP assays [17, 18, 19], the bottleneck extraction for more complicated sample types is still not solved. In terms of multiplexing, the Biofire FilmArray system for multiplex PCR [20] has already demonstrated that spatial multiplexing is preferential to one‐pot multiplexing, which is true for the workload needed to balance one‐pot reactions and for the verification and validation effort for one‐pot reactions versus spatially separated individual reactions. It is therefore to be expected that the simple multi use POCT devices will also move in this direction. Only a few device publications have listed cost of goods (CoGS) for isothermal and portable PCR devices (range 50–193$ per device [21, 22]), therefore, with a margin added it is safe to estimate the CoGs within 250€ for the above devices. They can be categorized as environmentally friendly as at least the minoo device was verified to be functional for at least 1000 runs [15]. If they solve the extraction issue, these simple readers could help to provide molecular diagnostics for infectious agents to the 47% of the global population that has little to no access to diagnostics at all, thus solving the last mile problem in providing access to diagnostics close to the patient [23]. In principle, these test platforms would be deliverable to users at reduced sales prices if upscaled production was outsourced to international electronics/mobile phone manufacturers. Local biochemistry production would allow dissemination of affordable respective assays close to the WHO requirement of 1$/test [13]. In comparison, current microfluidic and microsystem POCT systems in general fail to consider the economy of scale for mass production and market [24]. RPA has been rated as the most promising isothermal molecular amplification technique since it utilizes unmodified oligonucleotides, rapidly amplifies targets at only slightly elevated temperature without compromising the stringency of amplification, and uses probe‐based target verification in its real time format [1]. A meta‐analysis of molecular POC assays for SARS‐CoV‐2 concluded that seven RT‐RPA/RAA assays achieved detection sensitivity level similar to diagnosis on purified RNA samples by PCR from crude patient samples [25]. RPA was used in multiple field studies in mobile laboratories and produced sufficient evidence demonstrating that the performance of RPA is suitable for point of care use. In view of original RPA patents running out in 2026 the first open‐source protocols for RPA mix production have been published [26, 27]. Apart from the original Twist DX kit which currently is not available for RNA detection, three RPA copy chemistries are available in China: Recombinase Aided Amplification (RAA [28], Qitian, https://en.qt‐bio.com/Pro/12.html), Enzymatic Recombinase Amplification (ERA [29], GenDX, https://www.igeneye.com/), and Multienzyme Isothermal Rapid Amplification (MIRA [30], Amp‐Future Biotech Co. Ltd. https://www.amp‐futurebio.com/products). The impetus to copy the successful RPA concept goes even as far as claiming to have invented a probe system which is identical to the one originally published in 2006 [31]. In the area of lateral flow detection RPA is beginning to overtake LAMP with 490 publications versus 412 recorded on PubMed. Taken together RPA is catching up on LAMP (Figure 1) and has the potential to develop into a serious candidate for POCT implementation which is certainly the view in Asia as 61% of RPA publications originate from China alone. Manfred Weidmann previously worked in the startup midge medical GmbH, which developed the minoo device. The startup went into administration and ceased operations in 2024. title_original: Point of Care Testing and Recombinase Polymerase Amplification

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to explore the potential of Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) as a point-of-care (POCT) diagnostic tool, particularly in comparison to other isothermal amplification methods like LAMP, and to address the challenges in achieving sensitive and scalable POCT solutions for infectious diseases.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study reviewed existing literature and analyzed the design, performance, and application of RPA and related isothermal amplification methods in the context of POCT, focusing on their sensitivity, multiplexing capabilities, and environmental impact. It also examined the development of POCT devices for various pathogens, including SARS-CoV-2.
analysis.methods: The study evaluated the methods used in RPA and LAMP assays, including their sensitivity, multiplexing strategies, and the use of electronic components in POCT devices. It also considered the cost of goods for these devices and their environmental impact based on available literature.
analysis.main_results: The study found that RPA and LAMP have comparable sensitivity to real-time PCR, but RT-RPA sometimes struggles with sensitivity. It also noted that simple multi-use POCT devices like minoo, CPod, and Pebble have emerged, with the minoo device verified for at least 1000 runs.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpret that RPA is gaining traction as a viable POCT option, especially in Asia, and that the development of simple, cost-effective, and environmentally friendly devices could address the last-mile problem in diagnostics access.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that RPA could be a promising tool for POCT, particularly for pathogens like mpox, and that advancements in device design may improve diagnostic accessibility in low-resource settings.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The study is limited by its reliance on existing literature and the lack of direct experimental data on RPA's performance for mpox. The evidence is moderate, as it synthesizes findings from multiple studies rather than presenting original data.

analysis.summary_en: This study explores the potential of Recombinase Polymerase Amplification (RPA) as a point-of-care (POCT) diagnostic tool, comparing it to other isothermal amplification methods like LAMP. It highlights the challenges in achieving sensitive and scalable POCT solutions, particularly for infectious diseases. The study notes that RPA has comparable sensitivity to real-time PCR but may face issues with sensitivity when combined with reverse transcriptase. It also discusses the development of simple, multi-use POCT devices such as minoo, CPod, and Pebble, emphasizing their environmental impact and potential for improving diagnostic access. The authors suggest that RPA is gaining traction as a viable POCT option, especially in Asia, and that advancements in device design could address the last-mile problem in diagnostics. However, the study is limited by its reliance on existing literature and the absence of direct experimental data on RPA's performance for mpox, resulting in moderate evidence strength.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在探讨重组酶聚合酶扩增(RPA)作为床边检测(POCT)诊断工具的潜力,特别是在与其他等温扩增方法如LAMP的比较中,并解决在传染病领域实现灵敏且可扩展的POCT解决方案的挑战。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究回顾了现有文献,分析了RPA及相关等温扩增方法在床边检测(POCT)背景下的设计、性能和应用,重点关注其灵敏度、多重扩增能力以及环境影响。还考察了针对多种病原体(包括SARS-CoV-2)的POCT设备开发情况。
elements_zh.methods: 本研究评估了RPA和LAMP检测方法中使用的手段,包括其灵敏度、多重扩增策略以及POCT设备中电子元件的应用。还基于现有文献考虑了这些设备的成本和环境影响。
elements_zh.main_results: 本研究发现,RPA和LAMP的灵敏度与实时PCR相当,但RT-RPA(实时RPA)有时在灵敏度上存在困难。还注意到,像minoo、CPod和Pebble这样的简单多用途POCT设备已经出现,其中minoo设备已验证可运行至少1000次。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者认为,RPA正逐渐成为一种可行的POCT选项,尤其是在亚洲地区。开发简单、成本效益高且环保的设备可能有助于解决诊断可及性中的最后一公里问题。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 研究结果表明,RPA可能是POCT的有力工具,特别是对于像猴痘这样的病原体,设备设计的进展可能提高低资源环境下的诊断可及性。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 本研究的局限性在于其依赖现有文献,且缺乏对RPA在猴痘病原体上的直接实验数据。证据强度中等,因为其综合了多个研究的结果,而非提供原始数据。

title: Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research

source_records.title: Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research

full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02489-y Comment Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research Pontiano Kaleebu, Aliya Naheed, Mahnaz Vahedi, Jackeline Alger, Lyda Osorio, Cristiani Vieira Machado, Francine Ntoumi, Mercedes Rumi, Mohammed AlKhaldi, Pacifique Ndishimye, Evelyn Gitau & Trudie Lang Platforms for community-led but globally connected knowledge and resource sharing can move us towards more equitable and more effective research and solutions for infectious diseases. The burden of infectious disease is vast and global, yet research capac- ity remains starkly unequal around the world. Most infectious disease research funding goes to high-income countries, where research agendas are set, studies led and benefits realized1. Meanwhile, major endemic diseases such as tuberculosis, malaria and cholera dispropor- tionately affect the poorest, least resourced communities, and newer or re-emerging threats such as Ebola, Zika and mpox occur in settings least equipped to respond. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored that research is the pathway out of a pandemic. This is just as true for tackling long-standing infec- tious diseases. An entire connected ecosystem encompassing different types of research is needed to make progress: basic and preclinical research to understand pathogens and host responses; observational studies to assess disease impact and guide public health strategies; infectious disease surveillance and modelling to monitor trends and inform responses; clinical trials to test safety and efficacy of vaccines, therapeutics or preventive public health measures; and social and behavioural research to understand community perceptions shap- ing health behaviours such as treatment-seeking and antibiotic use. When these clinical, social and laboratory sciences are possible in every setting, responses to infectious disease threats are fairer, faster and more effective. Knowledge exchange can help overcome persistent health research equity barriers Despite the clear need for connected and inclusive research glob- ally, multiple barriers prevent many of the places most affected by infectious diseases from being able to lead their own research. These include gaps in core research competencies, such as methods, data management, community engagement and communication, as well as ethics and integrity2. Moreover, fragmentation and short-term approaches are an issue for locally led research across disease areas and research modalities, highlighting a need for scientific skill devel- opment3. Capacity-strengthening efforts are often tied to individual research projects and limited-term funding. While these initiatives can build important skills, they may lack the continuity and adapt- ability needed to develop transferable competencies that support longer-term independent research4. Structural constraints, such as chronic under-resourcing of research systems, further impede the routine adoption of newer tools, including federated data analysis, novel trial designs and genomics-informed surveillance. Alongside the need to develop scientific skills and strengthen research systems, improved financing, infrastructure, workforce development, govern- ance and operational systems are needed to embed research into rou- tine healthcare delivery and enable local evidence generation with the potential to drive immediate improvements in local health outcomes. Giving health workers a mandate and strengthening local research systems can help address some parts of the cycle of dependency upon external parties. To respond to this issue and support locally led research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), The Global Health Network (TGHN) was established in 2008. TGHN is a research practice-focused platform that was developed to aggregate, standard- ize and disseminate operational know-how across organizations, disci- plines, diseases and geographies, with the aim of helping individuals, groups and institutions move beyond dependency and one-off, focused projects into independent research. TGHN’s founding principle was to facilitate mobilization of research methods between researchers, and the platform is led through a franchise governance model with regional and country coordination. TGHN was first adopted in Africa, then rapidly developed into what is now a franchise community of more than 60 partners in more than 30 country centres across Latin America and the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia and, more recently, the Middle East and North Africa. Each region locally coordinates its own agendas and priorities, and runs locally relevant in-person knowledge-sharing activities that provide ongoing mentoring and guidance, such as research clubs (regular peer-learning discussions), workshops (skills-based training) and topic-specific clinics (expert-led sessions on specific research chal- lenges). TGHN is accessed by more than 1.25 million researchers and health worker members globally. It works in partnership with global and regional initiatives, including the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP3) and the Science for Africa Foundation, among others, and is a World Health Organization (WHO) Collaborating Centre for knowledge mobilization and capacity strengthening. The vast, connected TGHN community offers practical, free materials and peer support that directly address the workforce, procedural and gov- ernance gaps left unresolved by short-term projects. Fundamentally, TGHN connects researchers and research organizations to ensure that a researcher in a LMIC has access to the same knowledge and opportuni- ties as peers in high-income countries. Upskilling the health research workforce To better enable research in communities and disease areas where evidence is lacking, TGHN addresses several of the barriers described above. These include gaps in core research competencies, fragmented Check for updates nature microbiology Comment capacity-strengthening efforts and limited local leadership in identify- ing and addressing research priorities. Franchise-style governance, as implemented by TGHN, enables regional hubs to lead activities, adapt materials to their own context and identify their priorities. Combined with access to shared tools, standard training curricula and centrally curated quality assurance guidance, this strengthens research competencies and gives local teams the mandate and confidence to develop context-appropriate protocols, lead continuing professional development and generate evidence that directly addresses their health needs. By expanding opportunities beyond high-income country research centres and senior clinicians, local custodians are better equipped to generate context-specific evidence, making the immediate implemen- tation of practice innovations more feasible. Embedded research for everyday diseases also enables teams to spot new threats. For example, during the mpox outbreak in the African Great Lakes region, TGHN members came together to report an unusual clinical presentation and transmission pattern for the disease, to connect researchers and funders, and to enable the deployment of international-standard pro- tocols. Skills training and cross-border sharing supported rapid, locally led evidence generation and raised awareness and understanding of what turned out to be a new strain5. Similarly, during the 2016 Zika outbreak in Latin America, local teams accessed multilingual training and community engagement frameworks. When mistrust and poor participant retention were jeopardizing pregnancy cohort studies, TGHN connected these teams directly with researchers in Malawi experienced in pregnancy research. The Malawi team shared their approaches of engaging community health workers, advisory groups and influential family members to build trust and community support. The Latin American teams adapted these approaches locally, overcom- ing mistrust and resolving the retention challenges, enabling the Zika studies to continue6. Genomics and data science have transformed research in wealthier nations; however, they remain underused in LMICs7,8. Enabling broader adoption of advanced technology and data science is also a key part of TGHN’s aim to overcome barriers to equitable research. Cutting-edge tools and methods need to be adapted to make them relevant, acces- sible and usable in LMICs. This involves not only transferring technol- ogy but also interpreting discoveries (such as new pathogen variants) within local epidemiological and social contexts to guide policy and practice. TGHN’s Antimicrobial Resistance (AMR) Knowledge Hub is one resource that exemplifies such an attempt. This free and open com- munity gives researchers, including those based in LMICs, a platform to connect with others gathering data to tackle AMR. High-quality resources and globally recommended protocols and methods, for example, from the WHO, are shared, enabling locally relevant data to inform local and global strategies. By June 2026, the AMR Knowl- edge Hub had 19,057 members who had downloaded more than 669 resources, and had run activities including symposia across Latin America, Africa and Asia during World AMR Awareness Week9. For example, the Accuracy and consequences of using trial-of-antibiotics for tuberculosis diagnosis (ACT TB) team in Malawi demonstrated through a randomized trial that routine broad-spectrum antibiotic use during tuberculosis investigation provided limited diagnostic benefit without improving clinical outcomes, supporting its discontinua- tion and improved antimicrobial stewardship. The team shared their protocols, standard operating procedures and regulatory and ethics materials through the Hub, enabling other research teams to directly reuse and adapt these approaches10. Enabling community involvement in setting pandemic and outbreak response research agendas During the COVID-19 pandemic, TGHN’s Knowledge Hub provided critical virtual support to LMIC researchers across seven thematic areas: intervention trials, diagnostics, disease characterization, social sciences, ethics and community engagement, vaccines and health systems. It offered curated free resources, articles, toolkits, funding guidance and e-learning. Specifically, more than 200,000 COVID-19 research resources were downloaded. A crowdsourcing initiative was also hosted to openly share study protocols, standard operating pro- cedures, consent forms and other tools adapted for immediate uptake and use across the globe. Partnerships with organizations such as CEPI, the Public Health Emergency Preparedness and Response Ethics Network (PHEPREN), the UK Public Health Rapid Support Team (UK-PHRST) and the COVID Neuro Network (Brain Infections Global) have enabled more than 65 multilingual webinars and workshops covering a broad range of COVID- 19 research topics, as these organizations knew they could engage with research teams in LMICs through our network. These were attended by more than 45,000 participants. CEPI also used TGHN as the access point for COVAX, the focal point for global vaccine access. Armed with access to this information and new connections, the Network’s partners and members ran studies to address new questions and used data tools they had not previously known existed. TGHN members are highly engaged, so this community also offers the opportunity to ask questions to better understand the perspectives and priorities of researchers and practitioners in LMICs. For exam- ple, in May 2020, a study was conducted to gauge the global research community’s agreement with the WHO COVID-19 research roadmap11. The research community’s priority questions differed from those in the WHO’s COVID Blueprint roadmap. TGHN brought these findings, together with perspectives from its ongoing working groups, into its advisory work with the UK Government during its G7 presidency, suc- cessfully using this evidence to argue for a focus on strengthening the wider research ecosystem rather than on trials and product develop- ment alone. This work led to World Health Assembly Resolution 75.8 on strengthening clinical trials, which reflected this broader focus12. This ‘crowdsourced’ approach is possible due to the size of the TGHN community, and provides a platform for the viewpoint of those from the regions and roles most affected but often not represented. Since this COVID-19 initiative, other organizations have also engaged the TGHN community to identify research priorities, while ensuring that the perspectives of researchers and health workers from underrepresented settings are included. For example, a recent global mixed-methods study gathered perspectives from 3,752 TGHN mem- bers to identify infectious diseases at risk of escalation and the factors driving these risks, providing evidence to inform the organization’s research priorities13. Working together for equitable research All researchers, regardless of location, should have the tools, guidance, support, networks and knowledge needed to conduct high-quality research. Many organizations, such as the WHO, the Special Pro- gramme for Research and training in Tropical Diseases (TDR), EDCTP3, CEPI, the National Institute for Health and Care Research, the Well- come Trust and the Science for Africa Foundation, are also working to address these long-standing inequities, yet persistent barriers remain. Sustainable, flexible funding remains a critical need, par- ticularly for early-career researchers and for institutions without nature microbiology Comment long-standing donor ties. Structural inequities in authorship, lead- ership and research agenda-setting persist and must be dismantled. Weak infrastructure, the digital divide and limited access to scientific publishing continue to hold back progress, all well-documented and long-lamented disadvantages. By breaking down silos, upskilling the research workforce and linking marginalized communities to global resources, TGHN is actively working to address these barriers and create a fairer and more effective global health research ecosystem through the efforts of its global part- ners and members. Achieving this vision demands coordinated invest- ment across sectors: increased core funding for capacity-building in LMICs, partnerships that shift decision-making power, integration of research into health system planning, and stronger bridges between research, practice and policy. Sustaining and expanding these locally led, globally connected research communities can help ensure that the capacity to generate evidence exists where it is needed, enabling faster, more relevant and more equitable responses to current and future infectious disease threats. full_text_sections.full_text: nature microbiology https://doi.org/10.1038/s41564-026-02489-y Comment Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research Pontiano Kaleebu, Aliya Naheed, Mahnaz Vahedi, Jackeline Alger, Lyda Osorio, Cristiani Vieira Machado, Francine Ntoumi, Mercedes Rumi, Mohammed AlKhaldi, Pacifique Ndishimye, Evelyn Gitau & Trudie Lang Platforms for community-led but globally connected knowledge and resource sharing can move us towards more equitable and more effective research and solutions for infectious diseases. The burden of infectious disease is vast and global, yet research capac- ity remains starkly unequal around the world. Most infectious disease research funding goes to high-income countries, where research agendas are set, studies led and benefits realized1. Meanwhile, major endemic diseases such as tuberculosis, malaria and cholera dispropor- tionately affect the poorest, least resourced communities, and newer or re-emerging threats such as Ebola, Zika and mpox occur in settings least equipped to respond. The COVID-19 pandemic underscored that research is the pathway out of a pandemic. This is just as true for tackling long-standing infec- tious diseases. An entire connected ecosystem encompassing different types of research is needed to make progress: basic and preclinical research to understand pathogens and host responses; observational studies to assess disease impact and guide public health strategies; infectious disease surveillance and modelling to monitor trends and inform responses; clinical trials to test safety and efficacy of vaccines, therapeutics or preventive public health measures; and social and behavioural research to understand community perceptions shap- ing health behaviours such as treatment-seeking and antibiotic use. When these clinical, social and laboratory sciences are possible in every setting, responses to infectious disease threats are fairer, faster and more effective. Knowledge exchange can help overcome persistent health research equity barriers Despite the clear need for connected and inclusive research glob- ally, multiple barriers prevent many of the places most affected by infectious diseases from being able to lead their own research. These include gaps in core research competencies, such as methods, data management, community engagement and communication, as well as ethics and integrity2. Moreover, fragmentation and short-term approaches are an issue for locally led research across disease areas and research modalities, highlighting a need for scientific skill devel- opment3. Capacity-strengthening efforts are often tied to individual research projects and limited-term funding. While these initiatives can build important skills, they may lack the continuity and adapt- ability needed to develop transferable competencies that support longer-term independent research4. Structural constraints, such as chronic under-resourcing of research systems, further impede the routine adoption of newer tools, including federated data analysis, novel trial designs and genomics-informed surveillance. Alongside the need to develop scientific skills and strengthen research systems, improved financing, infrastructure, workforce development, govern- ance and operational systems are needed to embed research into rou- tine healthcare delivery and enable local evidence generation with the potential to drive immediate improvements in local health outcomes. Giving health workers a mandate and strengthening local research systems can help address some parts of the cycle of dependency upon external parties. To respond to this issue and support locally led research in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), The Global Health Network (TGHN) was established in 2008. TGHN is a research practice-focused platform that was developed to aggregate, standard- ize and disseminate operational know-how across organizations, disci- plines, diseases and geographies, with the aim of helping individuals, groups and institutions move beyond dependency and one-off, focused projects into independent research. TGHN’s founding principle was to facilitate mobilization of research methods between researchers, and the platform is led through a franchise governance model with regional and country coordination. TGHN was first adopted in Africa, then rapidly developed into what is now a franchise community of more than 60 partners in more than 30 country centres across Latin America and the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia and, more recently, the Middle East and North Africa. Each region locally coordinates its own agendas and priorities, and runs locally relevant in-person knowledge-sharing activities that provide ongoing mentoring and guidance, such as research clubs (regular peer-learning discussions), workshops (skills-based training) and topic-specific clinics (expert-led sessions on specific research chal- lenges). TGHN is accessed by more than 1.25 million researchers and health worker members globally. It works in partnership with global and regional initiatives, including the Coalition for Epidemic Preparedness Innovations (CEPI), the European and Developing Countries Clinical Trials Partnership (EDCTP3) and the Science for Africa Foundation, among others, and is a World Health Organization (WHO) Collaborating Centre for knowledge mobilization and capacity strengthening. The vast, connected TGHN community offers practical, free materials and peer support that directly address the workforce, procedural and gov- ernance gaps left unresolved by short-term projects. Fundamentally, TGHN connects researchers and research organizations to ensure that a researcher in a LMIC has access to the same knowledge and opportuni- ties as peers in high-income countries. Upskilling the health research workforce To better enable research in communities and disease areas where evidence is lacking, TGHN addresses several of the barriers described above. These include gaps in core research competencies, fragmented Check for updates nature microbiology Comment capacity-strengthening efforts and limited local leadership in identify- ing and addressing research priorities. Franchise-style governance, as implemented by TGHN, enables regional hubs to lead activities, adapt materials to their own context and identify their priorities. Combined with access to shared tools, standard training curricula and centrally curated quality assurance guidance, this strengthens research competencies and gives local teams the mandate and confidence to develop context-appropriate protocols, lead continuing professional development and generate evidence that directly addresses their health needs. By expanding opportunities beyond high-income country research centres and senior clinicians, local custodians are better equipped to generate context-specific evidence, making the immediate implemen- tation of practice innovations more feasible. Embedded research for everyday diseases also enables teams to spot new threats. For example, during the mpox outbreak in the African Great Lakes region, TGHN members came together to report an unusual clinical presentation and transmission pattern for the disease, to connect researchers and funders, and to enable the deployment of international-standard pro- tocols. Skills training and cross-border sharing supported rapid, locally led evidence generation and raised awareness and understanding of what turned out to be a new strain5. Similarly, during the 2016 Zika outbreak in Latin America, local teams accessed multilingual training and community engagement frameworks. When mistrust and poor participant retention were jeopardizing pregnancy cohort studies, TGHN connected these teams directly with researchers in Malawi experienced in pregnancy research. The Malawi team shared their approaches of engaging community health workers, advisory groups and influential family members to build trust and community support. The Latin Ameri…

title_original: Advancing equity through community-led, globally connected infectious disease research

analysis.research_question_and_background: The study aimed to address the global inequity in infectious disease research, particularly highlighting the disproportionate impact of diseases like mpox on low- and middle-income countries (LMICs) and the need for more equitable research practices.
analysis.study_design_and_population: The study involved a community-led, globally connected research platform called The Global Health Network (TGHN), which operates in multiple regions and countries, including Africa, Latin America and the Caribbean, South and Southeast Asia, and the Middle East and North Africa. It focused on research teams in LMICs, particularly those working on mpox and other infectious diseases.
analysis.methods: The methods included establishing partnerships with global initiatives such as CEPI and PHEPREN, organizing multilingual webinars and workshops, and facilitating knowledge exchange to support local research capacity and independence.
analysis.main_results: The TGHN platform successfully enabled over 65 multilingual webinars and workshops on various infectious disease topics, including mpox, and connected research teams with expertise in specific areas like pregnancy cohort studies. It also supported a randomized trial demonstrating the limited diagnostic benefit of using broad-spectrum antibiotics for tuberculosis, which informed antimicrobial stewardship practices.
analysis.interpretation_and_novelty: The authors interpreted these findings as evidence that collaborative, community-led research platforms can overcome systemic barriers and enable more effective, locally driven responses to infectious disease threats, including mpox. This approach is novel in its emphasis on embedding research into routine healthcare delivery and fostering local evidence generation.
analysis.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: The findings suggest that strengthening local research systems and fostering partnerships can improve the detection and response to emerging infectious diseases like mpox, leading to more equitable and effective public health strategies.
analysis.limitations_and_evidence_strength: The evidence is based on a single study and relies on reported outcomes from partnerships and webinars, which may lack direct, target-specific experimental data. However, the study provides a strong rationale for the importance of community-led research in addressing global health inequities.

analysis.summary_en: This study highlights the need for equitable and effective infectious disease research, particularly in low- and middle-income countries (LMICs), where diseases like mpox disproportionately affect communities. It describes the establishment of The Global Health Network (TGHN) as a community-led platform aimed at strengthening local research capacity and enabling independent, locally driven research. The methods involved partnerships with global initiatives, knowledge exchange, and capacity-building efforts. The main results include the successful organization of over 65 multilingual webinars and workshops, as well as a randomized trial showing limited diagnostic benefit of broad-spectrum antibiotics for tuberculosis. The authors interpret these findings as evidence that collaborative, community-led research can overcome systemic barriers and improve public health responses. The study suggests that such platforms can enhance the detection and management of infectious diseases like mpox, leading to more equitable health outcomes. However, the evidence is based on reported outcomes and partnerships, which may limit the strength of the findings.

elements_zh.research_question_and_background: 本研究旨在解决全球传染病研究中的不平等现象,特别是突出像猴痘这样的疾病对低收入和中等收入国家(LMICs)不成比例的影响,并强调需要更加公平的研究实践。
elements_zh.study_design_and_population: 本研究涉及一个名为全球健康网络(TGHN)的社区主导、全球互联的研究平台,该平台在多个地区和国家运营,包括非洲、拉丁美洲和加勒比地区、南亚和东南亚以及中东和北非。它重点关注在LMICs中从事猴痘和其他传染病研究的团队。
elements_zh.methods: 方法包括与全球倡议(如CEPI和PHEPREN)建立合作伙伴关系,组织多语言网络研讨会和研讨会,并促进知识交流以支持本地研究能力和独立性。
elements_zh.main_results: TGHN平台成功举办了超过65个多语言网络研讨会和研讨会,涵盖各种传染病主题,包括猴痘,并将具有特定领域专业知识的研究团队(如妊娠队列研究研究)连接起来。它还支持了一项随机试验,证明使用广谱抗生素对结核病的诊断益处有限,这为抗菌药物管理实践提供了信息。
elements_zh.interpretation_and_novelty: 作者将这些发现解释为证据,表明协作的、社区主导的研究平台可以克服系统性障碍,使对传染病威胁(包括猴痘)的应对更加有效且由本地驱动。这种方法的新颖之处在于其强调将研究嵌入常规医疗保健服务中,并促进本地证据的产生。
elements_zh.scientific_and_public_health_significanc: 这些发现表明,加强本地研究体系并促进合作伙伴关系可以提高对像猴痘这样的新兴传染病的检测和应对能力,从而推动更加公平和有效的公共卫生策略。
elements_zh.limitations_and_evidence_strength: 这些证据基于一项单一研究,并依赖于合作伙伴和网络研讨会报告的结果,这可能缺乏直接、针对性的实验数据。然而,该研究为社区主导研究在解决全球健康不平等问题中的重要性提供了有力的论据。
